message.content:
You are black-box reverse-engineering a compiled C++ binary. You MUST NOT look for or read any C++ library source (there is none on disk; `idna.hpp` does not exist). Derive behavior ONLY by running the binary.

BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable
Invoke as: /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "<domain-string>"
It prints exactly 4 lines, each "1" or "0", in this order:
  line1 = idna::is_valid_domain(input)
  line2 = idna::is_valid_label(input)
  line3 = idna::is_ascii_domain(input)
  line4 = idna::is_idn_domain(input)
With no argument, input defaults to the literal string "example.com".

ENVIRONMENT NOTES (important):
- python3 / python are NOT installed. perl may not be installed.
- Use bash loops, printf, tr, head, sed, awk to build test strings.
- Handy helper you can paste:
    rep() { local n=$1 c=$2 s=""; for ((i=0;i<n;i++)); do s+="$c"; done; printf '%s' "$s"; }
  or:  s=$(head -c 64 /dev/zero | tr '\0' 'a')
- To emit arbitrary/high bytes use: printf '\xNN'  (bash $'...' quoting also works)
- rustc and cargo ARE available if you need a quick generator program.

ALREADY-ESTABLISHED FACTS (verify, do not blindly trust):
- "" (empty)        -> 0 0 1 0
- "example.com"     -> 1 1 1 0
- "例子.测试"        -> 1 1 0 1
- "a"x63            -> 1 1 1 0
- "a"x64            -> 1 0 1 0   (is_valid_label flips off above 63)
- "a"x255           -> 1 0 1 0
- "a"x256           -> 0 0 1 0   (is_valid_domain flips off above 255)
- "." ".." "a." ".a" "a..b" "-a.com" "a-.com" "a_b.com" "a b.com" "a/b.com" "*.com" -> all 1 1 1 0

Be rigorous and quantitative. Bisect every boundary you claim (test N-1, N, N+1). Report exact reproducible command lines as evidence.


ADVERSARIAL VERIFICATION TASK.
Another agent studied the dimension "cli-and-output" and proposes this rule about the binary:

  RULE: Output is independent of argv[0] (program name/symlink) and of locale (LC_ALL/LANG).
  Their claimed evidence: $ cd /workspace/dataset
$ cp test4_executable /tmp/renamed_thing && /tmp/renamed_thing | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n
$ ln -sf /workspace/dataset/test4_executable /tmp/lnk && /tmp/lnk | od -c
0000000   1  \n   1  \n   1  \n   0  \n
$ for L in C C.UTF-8 en_US.UTF-8 POSIX; do printf '%-12s %s\n' "$L" "$(LC_ALL=$L LANG=$L ./test4_executable | tr '\n' ',')"; done
C            1,1,1,0,
C.UTF-8      1,1,1,0,
en_US.UTF-8  1,1,1,0,
POSIX        1,1,1,0,

Your job is to REFUTE it. Actively hunt for a counterexample by running /workspace/dataset/test4_executable yourself. Do not take their evidence on faith — re-run it. Then attack:
 - boundary off-by-ones (test N-1, N, N+1 around every number in the rule)
 - bytes vs codepoints confusion if the rule mentions a length
 - non-ASCII / invalid-UTF-8 inputs
 - empty string and single-character inputs
 - whether the rule over-generalizes from a small sample

Set holds=false and give the exact counterexample input + observed 4-line output if you find one. If the rule is directionally right but imprecise, set holds=false and put a precise version in correctedStatement. Only set holds=true if you genuinely tried and failed to break it. Default to skepticism.

First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

content.text:
I ran an exhaustive hunt and could not break the rule. Here is my evidence.

## Reproduction of their evidence — confirmed
```
$ cp /workspace/dataset/test4_executable /tmp/renamed_thing && /tmp/renamed_thing | tr '\n' ','   -> 1,1,1,0,
$ ln -sf /workspace/dataset/test4_executable /tmp/lnk && /tmp/lnk | tr '\n' ','                    -> 1,1,1,0,
$ for L in C C.UTF-8 en_US.UTF-8 POSIX; do LC_ALL=$L LANG=$L ...                                   -> all 1,1,1,0,
```
But their evidence is weak: it used exactly **one** input (the default ASCII `example.com`) and 4 locales. Locale-sensitive `ctype` behavior can only manifest on high bytes, so their sample could not have detected a locale dependency. I re-tested properly.

## argv[0] attacks — all identical output
```
$ exec -a "" /workspace/dataset/test4_executable                     -> 1,1,1,0,
$ exec -a "--help" ...   /  "-"  /  "/"  /  "x"  /  $'a\xffb'         -> 1,1,1,0,
$ exec -a "$(head -c 100000 /dev/zero|tr '\0' Q)" ... "例子.测试"      -> 1,1,0,1,
$ ln -f  (hardlink) /tmp/hardlink_thing "例子.测试"                    -> 1,1,0,1,
$ cp -> /tmp/idna  and  /tmp/is_ascii_domain  (suggestive basenames)  -> 1,1,0,1,
```
The strongest case, which `exec -a` cannot produce — **argc == 0** (empty `argv[]` via raw `execve`, built with `rustc` at `/tmp/argc0/main3.rs`):
```
$ /tmp/argc0/run /workspace/dataset/test4_executable        # argc==0, empty envp
1 1 1 0     (still the "example.com" default)
```

## Locale attacks — 6912 + ~2400 runs, zero diffs
- **All 864 installed locales** (`locale -a`) × 8 discriminating inputs (`例子.测试`, `a\xffb.\xe9`, 21/22/85/86 × `中`, `EXAMPLE.COM`, `\xdf.de`), setting `LC_ALL`+`LANG`+`LC_CTYPE`+`LC_COLLATE`: **6912 runs, 0 diffs.**
- Every `LC_*` category individually (`LC_CTYPE`, `LC_COLLATE`, `LC_NUMERIC`, `LC_MESSAGES`, `LC_TIME`) plus `LANGUAGE` — 0 diffs.
- `env -i` (empty environment), `LOCPATH=/nonexistent`, `LOCPATH=/tmp`, `GCONV_PATH=/nonexistent`, `MALLOC_PERTURB_=170`, a 5000-byte `LC_ALL` value, and the invalid locale `bogus_LOCALE.xyz` — 0 diffs, stderr empty in all cases, exit code always 0.
- All 255 single bytes × 4 charset-diverse locales — 0 diffs.
- 250 random byte strings (incl. invalid UTF-8) × 6 locales — 0 diffs.

## The decisive test: locale-dependent length counting
Lengths are **byte**-based, and I confirmed the boundaries do not shift with locale. `中` is 3 bytes, so a byte-based 63 limit breaks at 22 chars (66 B) while a codepoint-based one would break at 64 chars:
```
chars=21 bytes=63  -> 1,1,0,1     chars=85 bytes=255 -> 1,0,0,1
chars=22 bytes=66  -> 1,0,0,1     chars=86 bytes=258 -> 0,0,0,1
```
If length used `mbstowcs`, a single-byte locale (`ru_RU.koi8r`, `tr_TR.iso88599`) would count 66 B as 66 chars while `en_US.utf8` counts 22 — the 63/255 boundaries would move. Tested chars = 20,21,22,23,62,63,64,84,85,86,87 and `a`×62/63/64/254/255/256 across 14 charset-diverse locales: **0 diffs.**

## Mechanistic confirmation
`readelf -Ws` shows the binary imports `tolower@GLIBC_2.2.5` (a locale-sensitive glibc function) but has **no `setlocale`/`localeconv`/`iconv`/`nl_langinfo` import**. Since the program never calls `setlocale(LC_ALL, "")`, the process stays in the `"C"` locale for its whole lifetime, so `tolower` uses the fixed C ctype table no matter what the environment says. This is a structural reason the rule holds, not a lucky sample.

## One adjacent precision note (does not refute the rule)
The rule is about `argv[0]`, and that is genuinely irrelevant — but the output *does* depend on **argc**: absent `argv[1]` yields the `example.com` default (`1 1 1 0`), whereas a present-but-empty `argv[1]` yields `0 0 1 0`. `argv[2..]` are ignored.
```
$ /tmp/argc0/run /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "zzz" ""   -> 0 0 1 0
$ /workspace/dataset/test4_executable "example.com" "例子.测试" "zzz" -> 1 1 1 0
```
